title: Transpose a tune up a fifth
summary: Move a short tune up a fifth two ways: find it by ear first, then check it against the rule.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil

figure.alt: A one-octave keyboard from middle C. C4 and G4 are highlighted, a fifth apart: the interval the tune moves up by ear first, then checked by counting seven keys, black keys included, from each original note.

steps.title: Transpose a tune up a fifth
steps.body:
A fifth higher means every note moves up seven keys, counting the black keys as well as the white ones. That comes out to a frequency ratio close to 3 to 2. Your ear can find the same answer without counting a single key.

1. Pick a four-bar tune you know well enough to hum without the page.
2. Try playing it starting a fifth higher, by ear, listening for the same shape of ups and downs.
3. Now check it by rule: count seven keys up from each original note, black keys included, and compare that to what you played.
4. Fix any note where your ear and the rule disagreed, and figure out which one was right.

Ear and rule should agree, because they are describing the same thing two different ways. When they do not, that is worth stopping to understand, not just fixing.

figure.alt: The same fifth, C4 to G4, highlighted on a one-octave keyboard: the seven-keys rule every transposed note is checked against, once the tune has been tried a fifth higher by ear.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: pick the tune, try it a fifth higher by ear
Sitting 2: check every note against the seven-keys rule, fix any that disagree
Sitting 3: play the transposed tune three times until it is smooth
Sitting 4: play the original and the transposed tune back to back, then as if recording
An old piece played once, in its original key

steps.title: Record this week's version
steps.prompt: Play the tune in its original key, then play it transposed up a fifth, in the same take, hands in the frame.

extras.title: A tune that transposes itself
extras.body:
Make up a four-bar tune that sounds right in more than one key.

Start with a question: what tune would still sound the same if every note moved up together?

Three constraints: use only five notes, keep one steady beat, and start and end on the same scale step.

Sketch first: write the note names on paper before you play them.

You know it works when you can play it in your first key, then a fifth higher, and both still sound right.
